title: 第13章 闽地密报第14章 托梦
content_zh:
夜深了，杜府主院的书房里还亮着灯。
杜茂源坐在桌案后，面前摊着一封刚从闽地送来的密报。
烛火将他的影子投在墙上，忽大忽小，像一头困兽在笼子里来回踱步。
密报上字不多，但每个字都让他如坐针毡。
“未收到货，亦未见船。”
杜茂源的手指微微发颤，将那张纸凑到烛火上。
火舌舔上纸的一角，整张纸立刻卷曲起来，很快化作一捧灰烬，飘落在砚台边。
他盯着那捧灰烬看了许久，仿佛看到自己的前程，一片晦暗。
本朝开国至今，节度使的任命早就不看战功了。家底殷实的自己掏钱，没钱的就去借，以数倍的利息向富室举债，凑足了贿赂送上，等到了方镇，再疯狂搜刮民财来还债。
他杜茂源当年就是这么上来的。
他杜茂源能坐到泾原节度使的位置，靠的不是军功，是人情，更准确地说，是钱。
这事说起来不光彩，可是朝堂上下，谁不是这么干的？
在本朝，这不是秘密，是规矩。
可是规矩，因人而变。
他的靠山已经岌岌可危，他不得不另谋出路，寻找更大的靠山，好保全自己，不让自己成为城门失火殃及池鱼的鱼。
于是，他好不容易搭上了闽地驻军的线。
然而，第一艘满载他前途的船却沉在东海，说是遇到海匪，财物尽失，人船俱毁。
小女杜若也差点丧命。
他还是高看了这个将门虎女的后代。
他以为孟氏是将门之女，杜若也有将门之后的风范，天生该是办这种事的料。

这丫头为了樊义山的婚事又自告奋勇，他便特意安排了走访闽地亲戚的名义，又派了满船的高手护送，以为万无一失，没想到还是船毁人亡，财物尽失，到底是谁走漏了风声？
而现在，这第二艘船还没来得及派。
他已经不敢再轻易冒险了，可驻军那边的催促又像催命符一样，一天比一天急。
“老爷。”
门外响起了杜安的声音，小心翼翼的，像是怕惊动了什么。
杜茂源收敛了神色，端起桌上的茶盏，抿了一口茶，已经凉了，涩得他舌根发苦。
“进来。”杜茂源道。
杜安推门进来，弓着身子，手里提着一个食盒，轻手轻脚地放在桌角。
“这几日夫人的后事辛苦你了。”杜茂源头也没抬。
“这不是奴才分内的事吗？”杜安顿了顿，“五娘子白日里哭了好几场，方才才歇下。”
杜茂源没有接话。
柳氏死了，死得突然，死得蹊跷，七窍流血，仵作说是抱病而亡，可杜茂源心里清楚。
柳氏的身体一向硬朗，前一日还在张罗着去大相国寺上香，怎么回来就……
他没有继续想下去，有些事想多了反而不安生。
柳氏死了，府里少了一个多嘴多舌的人，未必是坏事，上次杜若押船的事消息是怎么走漏的？驻军那边问询时，言语间暗示有人通风报信，是谁？
知道这件事的人不多，柳氏算一个。
现在他死了，死无对证。
杜茂源端起茶盏，将杯中凉透的茶一饮而尽，喉结上下滚动了一下。
“老爷，”杜安又开口了，声音压得更低，“东海那边今日又来了信……”
杜茂源的手微微一颤。

杜安从袖中取出一封信，双手呈上信封。
没有落款，只在封口处压了一道火漆，上面盖着一个他不认识的印章。
杜茂源接过信也不急着拆，只是用指腹摩挲着那道火漆，像是在掂量里面装的是催命的符，还是救命的药。
content_en:
It was late at night, and the lights were still on in the study room in the main courtyard of Du Mansion.
Du Maoyuan sat behind the desk with a secret report just sent from Fujian spread out in front of him.
The candlelight cast his shadow on the wall, suddenly large and small, like a trapped animal pacing back and forth in a cage.
There were not many words in the secret report, but every word made him sit on pins and needles.
"No goods received, no ship sighted."
Du Maoyuan's fingers trembled slightly as he held the piece of paper to the candlelight.
The tongue of fire licked a corner of the paper, and the whole paper immediately curled up, and soon turned into a handful of ashes, falling beside the inkstone.
He stared at the handful of ashes for a long time, as if he saw a gloomy future for himself.
Since the founding of this dynasty, the appointment of military governors has long been no longer based on military merit. Those who were well-off paid for it themselves, and those who had no money borrowed it. They borrowed money from wealthy families at multiple times of interest, collected enough bribes and sent them. When they got to Fang Town, they frantically plundered people's wealth to repay the debt.
This is how he, Du Maoyuan, came up.
He, Du Maoyuan, was able to sit in the position of Jingyuan Jiedushi, not because of military merit, but because of favors, and to be more precise, it was money.
It's a disgraceful thing to say, but who in the court wouldn't do this?
In this dynasty, this is not a secret, it is a rule.
But rules change depending on the person.
His backing was already in jeopardy, and he had to find another way out, looking for a bigger backing, so as to protect himself and prevent himself from becoming a fish in the pond when the city gate was on fire.
So, he finally got on the line with the troops stationed in Fujian.
However, the first ship that was full of his future sank in the East China Sea. It was said that it encountered pirates, and all his property was lost, and everyone on the ship was destroyed.
The younger daughter Du Ruo also almost died.
He still had a high regard for the descendant of this general's tiger girl.
He thought that Meng was the daughter of a general, and Du Ruo also had the demeanor of a general, so she was born to do this kind of thing.
This girl volunteered again for Fan Yishan's marriage, so he specially arranged to visit relatives in Fujian, and sent a boat full of experts to escort her. He thought everything was safe, but unexpectedly, the boat was destroyed, everyone was killed, and all property was lost. Who leaked the news?
But now, this second ship has not yet been dispatched.
He no longer dared to take risks easily, but the urging from the garrison was like a reminder, getting more urgent day by day.
"Master."
Duan's voice sounded outside the door, cautiously, as if he was afraid of disturbing something.
Du Maoyuan calmed down, picked up the tea cup on the table, and took a sip of the tea. It was already cold and astringent to the point where his tongue felt bitter.
"Come in." Du Maoyuan said.
Du An pushed the door open and came in, hunched over, holding a food box in his hand and placing it gently on the corner of the table.
"It's been hard on you these past few days for Madam's funeral." Du Mao didn't raise his voice.
"Isn't this a slave's duty?" Du An paused, "The fifth lady cried several times during the day, and she just rested."
Du Maoyuan didn't answer.
Mrs. Liu died suddenly and strangely, with bleeding from all her orifices. Gu Zuo said she died of illness, but Du Maoyuan knew it well.
Mrs. Liu's body has always been strong. The day before, she was making arrangements to go to Daxiangguo Temple to offer incense. Why did she come back...
He didn't continue to think about it. Some things made him uneasy if he thought about them too much.
Mrs. Liu is dead, and there is one less talkative person in the house, which is not necessarily a bad thing. How did the news about Du Ruo's escorting the ship leak out last time? When the garrison asked, they hinted that someone had tipped off the news. Who was it?
Not many people know about this matter, Liu is one of them.
Now that he is dead, there is no evidence of his death.
Du Maoyuan picked up the tea cup and drank the cool tea in one gulp, his Adam's apple rolling up and down.
"Master," Du An spoke again, his voice lowered, "Another letter came from the East China Sea today..."
Du Maoyuan's hand trembled slightly.
Duane took out a letter from his sleeve and presented the envelope with both hands.
There was no signature, only a line of lacquer on the seal, and a seal he didn't recognize stamped on it.
Du Maoyuan took the letter and was not in a hurry to open it. He just rubbed the letter with his fingertips.The fire paint seemed to be weighing whether it contained a life-saving charm or a life-saving medicine.
